q: Wind dropped a deep, pale, fine silt across the Danube valley during the ice ages, and whole hillsides east of the Wachau are buried in it. What is the material?
exp: Loess is windblown, calcareous and often many metres deep; it warms quickly and holds water, and it gives a broad, ripe, generous Gruner Veltliner. The lean, taut wines come off weathered primary rock further west, which is a wholly different proposition.

q: Mortarless walls of stacked stone hold the soil on the steepest Danube slopes, and growers rebuild them by hand. Beyond stopping the ground from sliding, what do they contribute?
opts: They channel irrigation water along each terrace
They store heat and release it at night
They mark the legal boundary of each single vineyard
They raise humidity around the fruit and encourage noble rot
exp: Stone is a heat store, so a terrace wall keeps working long after sunset and stretches a ripening day that has nothing to spare at this latitude. Botrytis is the last thing wanted here, since these wines are made dry and clean.

q: Ask an Austrian grower which federal state he farms in and the answer is nearly always one of four. Which four carry essentially all the country's vineyard?
exp: Lower Austria, Burgenland, Styria and Vienna hold the vineyards; the western and southern states have only token plantings, gathered for labelling purposes under the name Bergland. Vienna is the oddity, a capital with serious commercial vineyard inside its own boundary.

q: Wachau, Kamptal, Kremstal, Weinviertel and Carnuntum are all administered as parts of a single federal state. Which?
exp: Lower Austria wraps around Vienna and carries more vineyard than the other three states put together, divided into eight named regions. Burgenland runs south along the Hungarian border and Styria sits in the far south-east.

q: Three letters follow the region name on many Austrian labels and stand for a Latin phrase. What do they abbreviate?
exp: The Latin was chosen so the initials would sit comfortably beside AOC, DOC and DO on an international list. A DAC name may be used only for wine the region has agreed is typical of it, so the letters make a claim about style as well as about place.

q: Before the DAC scheme arrived, a Lower Austrian label led with the grape and treated the region as little more than an address. What did the scheme put in first place instead?
opts: A minimum time in cask before release, lengthening at each step up the ladder
A ranking of individual sites, so the finest Rieden could be named on a classified label
A yield ceiling set nationally, the same for every region and every variety
Typicity of origin, so a regional name goes only to wines judged typical
exp: The model is Romance rather than Germanic: the name of the place does the work, not the name of the grape. The typicity judgement rides on the state tasting every Qualitatswein already faces; what each region sets is the standard that tasting is measured against. Each DAC then decides which varieties and styles may carry its name, which is why the permitted grapes differ sharply from one to the next. Site ranking, yields and ageing are all settled region by region and came later; what the scheme changed first was whose name goes on the front of the label.

q: A Kamptal grower ferments a Sauvignon Blanc, a variety his DAC does not permit. What origin may that wine claim on its label?
opts: Kamptal, because the fruit was unquestionably grown there
Austria and nothing narrower, because the wine has lost quality status
Niederosterreich, the federal state, as the DAC name is closed to it
Kamptal Landwein, a lower tier of the same name
exp: A wine that falls outside its DAC drops back to the wider federal-state name, and that is precisely what makes the DAC name worth anything. The wine remains Qualitatswein and remains Kamptal fruit in fact; it simply may not say so.

q: Origin can be drawn at three widths inside an Austrian DAC, tightening from the whole district down to one named site. What are those three steps called?
exp: Gebiet is the district, Ort the village and Ried the individual vineyard, and yields and ripeness requirements tighten at each step up. Gutswein, Ortswein and Grosse Lage is Germany's VDP pyramid, and Klassik, Reserve and Grosse Reserve was the Austrian sparkling ladder before its 2022 rebranding. Both look similar to the DAC steps and mean something else entirely.

q: Four broad tiers stack Austrian wine law from the bottom upward. Which sequence is correct?
exp: The upper two tiers must come from a named region and pass a state analysis and a blind tasting before they receive an inspection number. Pradikatswein is then subdivided by must weight, and enrichment is forbidden throughout it.

q: A blue baroque church tower and the ruined castle where Richard the Lionheart was held look down over terraced vines beside the Danube. Which region?
exp: Durnstein sits in the middle of the Wachau, a thirty-kilometre stretch of river between Melk and Krems that UNESCO lists as a cultural landscape. The terraces are cut into weathered gneiss and granulite, and every operation on them is done by hand.

q: Two bottles come from one Wachau grower: one off weathered gneiss high on the terraces, one off deep loess near the river. What should a guest expect to taste?
opts: The primary-rock wine leaner and tauter, the loess wine broader and riper
The primary-rock wine broader and riper, the loess wine leaner and tauter
The loess wine sweet and the primary-rock wine dry
No difference worth naming, since both were made in the same cellar
exp: Urgestein is the local word for the ancient crystalline rock, and it holds almost no water, so the vine struggles and the wine stays tight and stony. Loess is deep and retentive, and it supplies the flesh that Wachau Gruner Veltliner is loved for.

q: The three ripeness words on a Wachau label are no part of Austrian wine law. Who set them, and under what?
opts: The European Union, under the region's protected designation
Vinea Wachau, a growers' association, under its own Codex Wachau
The federal wine authority, under the wine law of 1985
The Klosterneuburg research institute, under its must-weight scale
exp: The association formed in 1983 and its rules go well beyond the law: fruit only from the Wachau, no enrichment, no concentration and nothing added for aroma. Membership is voluntary, so a Wachau wine can be superb and carry none of the three words.

q: Wachau growers grade ripeness by the alcohol in the finished wine rather than by the sugar in the must. What makes that the sensible measure there?
opts: Austrian law forbids must-weight terms anywhere in Lower Austria
Must weight cannot be measured accurately on primary-rock soils
The wines are fermented dry, so ripeness becomes alcohol
The three terms record vineyard altitude rather than ripeness at all
exp: Germany's ladder works because the sugar survives into the bottle where it can be tasted; a bone-dry wine has spent all of it. Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd therefore read as a scale of weight and power on the palate.

q: Lightest of the Wachau's three categories, capped at eleven and a half percent alcohol and named after a feathery grass that seeds itself among the terraces. Which term?
exp: Stipa pennata, the feather grass, colonises the dry stone walls, and the wine named after it is meant to be drunk young and cold. Federspiel and Smaragd sit above it, and Kabinett belongs to the national system rather than to the Wachau.

q: The dinner-table weight of Wachau white runs between eleven and a half and twelve and a half percent alcohol. Which of the region's terms marks that band?
exp: Federspiel takes its name from the lure a falconer swings to call the bird back, a nod to the sport once practised on these cliffs. It is the classic food weight of the region: dry, precise and never heavy.

q: An emerald green lizard basking on a terrace wall lent its name to the ripest of the Wachau categories. Which category, and what does it demand?
opts: Steinfeder, which requires at least twelve and a half percent alcohol
Federspiel, which requires hand harvesting above all else
Smaragd, which requires at least twelve and a half percent alcohol
exp: Smaragd fruit is picked last and off the warmest terraces, and the wines are powerful, dry and capable of decades in bottle. Noble rot is not what any of these categories is chasing, which is why the botrytis version of the answer fails.
